# Phosphorus and friction matches (`phosphorus_matches`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by sulphuric_acid, distillation, chlorine_bleach
- Core idea: Phosphorus was first made by boiling stale urine down to a paste and heating it white-hot in a retort whose neck dips under water, where a waxy solid that glows in the dark collects; later from bone ash treated with sulphuric acid and heated with charcoal. A match needs a fuel, an oxygen-giving salt and a binder: the safe design puts potassium chlorate, sulphur or antimony sulphide and glue on the stick, and red phosphorus with powdered glass on the box, so that fire starts only when the two meet. Red phosphorus is made by heating the white form to about 250 °C without air.
- Pitfalls:
  - White phosphorus ignites in air near 30 °C, causes deep burns and is lethal at about a tenth of a gram; keep and cut it under water.
  - White-phosphorus match heads gave workers 'phossy jaw' (rotting jawbone) and poisoned children; use red phosphorus.
  - Grinding potassium chlorate together with sulphur or phosphorus: the mixture explodes from friction. Mix wet, never in a mortar.
  - Thinking a match is just sulphur on a stick; sulphur spills only carry a flame from an existing ember.
- History: china: AD 577 – sulphur-tipped pine sticks used by court ladies of Northern Qi; described c. 950 by Tao Gu. They need an ember and are not friction matches; europe: 1669 – Hennig Brand (Hamburg) from urine; 1769–1771 Gahn and Scheele from bone; 1826 John Walker's friction match (no phosphorus); 1830–1831 Sauria's white-phosphorus match; 1844 Pasch and 1855 Lundström, safety match; 1845 Schrötter (Vienna), red phosphorus; 1906 Berne Convention bans white-phosphorus matches
- Read:
  - John Emsley, The Shocking History of Phosphorus (2000)
  - M. F. Crass, A History of the Match Industry, Journal of Chemical Education 18 (1941)
